text: The farm still runs; the men who used to own it have simply become guests. Mario Monicelli's 1985 comedy hands a Tuscan estate to a divorced countess and lets her keep it, with her sisters, aunts and servants doing the actual work of animals, harvests and accounts while the count and his friends drift back in with plans. Liv Ullmann plays the woman at the centre, Philippe Noiret the husband who cannot quite grasp that his return changes nothing operational. Two hours is a lot of room, and Monicelli spends it on meals, arguments, chores, the slow accumulation of who reaches for what. The comedy is never about a woman proving she can manage. It is about the men discovering, one small competence at a time, that nobody was waiting.

A clerical slip sends a twelve-year-old with epilepsy to the psychiatric ward instead of the neurological one, and the film stays there. Francesca Archibugi builds ninety-eight minutes out of the consequences: Pippi among patients whose troubles are nothing like hers, doctors improvising, a family visiting a place they never expected. The mistake is not the crisis. What follows is, because a hospital that has filed a child wrongly has no procedure for noticing. Archibugi keeps the camera at a child's eye level and lets adult explanation arrive incomplete, the way it does. The Italian cinema of the early nineties had few pictures this patient about institutional care, and this one refuses the easy indignation the premise offers, choosing instead to watch what a wrong room does to a girl and the man assigned to her.

His father was an anti-Fascist, and in his town that inheritance is a sentence rather than an honor. Alberto Bevilacqua's first feature follows a man who leaves the community that raised him and marries a nobleman's daughter, which is one way of describing an escape and another way of describing a defection. The film runs nearly two hours and belongs to a moment when Italian cinema was still arguing directly with the Fascist decades, though here the argument is domestic: a marriage, a family with a name, a set of rooms in which the man's origins are known and politely unmentioned. What Bevilacqua is after is the daily cost of a decision that looked practical. Class in Italy is not abstract in this film; it is a father-in-law, a house, a way of holding a fork.

Brooklyn in the 1950s, a strike at the plant, and three lives that never quite intersect except in the same few blocks. Uli Edel's film moves between a union leader who discovers he is gay, a prostitute who makes the mistake of loving a client, and a family unable to absorb a daughter's pregnancy, and it declines to soften any of the three into a lesson. It was made in West Germany, in English, with American actors, which gives its Brooklyn a slight strangeness of address, a place reconstructed by people looking at it from outside. The result is 103 minutes with almost no relief in them. Nobody in it is punished for a flaw; they are simply held in a neighborhood, a decade, and an economy that have no use for what they want.

Thirty-two years in the Soviet Union, and then a boat back to a Greece that has moved on without him. Theo Angelopoulos gives the returning communist no welcome and no denunciation, only relatives with property questions, officials with forms, and a country that has finished the argument he never stopped having. The 139-minute running time is not incidental; Angelopoulos holds shots until waiting becomes the film's real subject, and the old man's exile continues on Greek soil in a different form. His son is a filmmaker, which lets the film watch itself trying to construct a father. What survives of a political life once the politics are historical is asked here in terms of paperwork, a mountain village, and a jetty in the rain, never in the language of ideas.

Two grandchildren go looking for a kamikaze pilot and come back with contradictions instead of a man. Takashi Yamazaki structures 144 minutes around interviews with the dead flier's surviving comrades, each of whom remembers a different person: a coward, a superb airman, someone who talked too much about coming home. The wartime scenes arrive as testimony rather than as record, which puts the film's considerable aerial spectacle inside quotation marks that it does not always keep closed. Japan has produced few blockbusters willing to leave a kamikaze this unresolved. The mystery is a genuine one, and the film's method is to let each veteran's account stand undisturbed until the next one damages it, leaving the siblings with a grandfather assembled from people who need him to have been something.

The daughter has never had a name she kept for more than a year. Christian Petzold's first cinema feature puts a family of German left-wing terrorists fifteen years into their flight, long past the politics that started it, reduced to rented rooms and cash and the discipline of never being interesting to anyone. Then fifteen-year-old Jeanne meets a boy on a beach and wants what any teenager wants, which is to be known. Petzold shoots the parents' vigilance as ordinary parenting pushed one degree past sense, so the film works as a study of adolescence and of the German Autumn's long residue at the same time. The threat here is not the police. It is a girl who has decided to exist, and the mother and father who must talk her out of it.

A woman alone in a mountain house in Bavaria, 1942, doing exercises and waiting for weekend guests. Aleksandr Sokurov films Eva Braun's few days with Adolf, Josef and Magda Goebbels and Martin Bormann as a country holiday from which politics has been formally excluded, which leaves small talk, walks, meals and boredom. He shoots it in Russian, in a green-grey haze that drains the Alps of their postcard, and the effect is neither satire nor indictment but something more uncomfortable: the historically monstrous rendered as tedious company. Eva is the film's consciousness, restless and unattended, circling men who have nothing to say when not permitted their subject. Its cinematography took a European Film Award, and the reason is visible in every frame, where fog does the work an accusation would have done.

A concert pianist cannot remember, and the men around her are all certain they know why. Britain in 1946 was working through a national fascination with psychiatry, and this film puts it on screen literally: a doctor, a case, and a life reconstructed in flashback while the patient sits mostly silent. The title's veil is a therapeutic conceit, the last covering that a mind will not lift, and the screenplay took an Academy Award for the way it turns that idea into structure. What makes it stranger than its melodrama surface is the piano. The woman's talent is treated by everyone as a possession to be managed, protected, invested in, and the hands that cannot play become the site where the argument over who owns her is finally conducted.

Tokyo Tower goes up a little more in each scene, visible from a street of small shops that will not survive the decade it announces. Takashi Yamazaki sets 1958 in a neighborhood of repairmen, a struggling novelist, a woman running a bar, children who work, and builds 133 minutes out of arrivals and debts and meals rather than any single plot. The digital reconstruction of postwar Tokyo is the film's engine and its argument at once: a vanished city rendered with more care than any surviving photograph allows, warmly and knowingly too clean. Japanese audiences took it as memory. What it actually offers is the moment before the boom, when a television set in a shop window could still gather a whole street, and modernization looked like something happening to other people.

In a Gujarati village the women walk to the well and back, and that walk is the only ground they are permitted. Abhishek Shah's film gives them a stranger in the desert and, through him, the garba — a dance they have been forbidden, performed where nobody can see. What follows is not a rebellion so much as a habit forming, an hour a day of something that belongs to them, and the village's men noticing that their wives have somewhere else to be. Shah shoots the Kutch desert as flat and enormous, so the circle of dancers becomes the only shape in the frame with a centre. The film is in Gujarati, a language with almost no presence in serious Indian cinema, and its subject is exactly that: what a form does when it is finally allowed a body.
